title: Building a Video Modal with the HTML Dialog Element | Part 6
description:
Today I worked on the markup and styles for the Responsive Video Gallery's video modal. I compared the HTML dialog element with the Popover API, reviewed a YouTube embed, and planned the data attributes that will identify each video's platform and ID. I used showModal() to open a sample dialog so I could style it, and added a close-button click handler to try the basic interaction.

Most of the CSS work centered on the backdrop, iframe sizing, and a close button that looks offset from the video while remaining inside the dialog. I used padding to make room for the button, styled its hover and focus states, and investigated why the iframe's proportions changed as the layout narrowed. I left that sizing issue for further testing rather than calling it solved. I also talked about project-based learning, freelance deliverables, and my plans for open-source and paid versions of frontend projects; dynamic gallery creation and Vimeo support are still future work.

- Learning frontend development by building projects

title: Building an Accessible Mobile Menu with Mostly CSS | Part 3
description:
Today I finished the Scenic footer and built almost the entire responsive navigation system with vanilla CSS. I styled shared form controls first, then added the newsletter-specific transparent inputs, contrasting submit button, hover and focus transitions, fluid padding and a mobile stack. I completed the social footer with embedded GitHub, Instagram, LinkedIn, Pinterest and X icons, large tap targets, accessible color changes and responsive spacing that remains tidy down to a 320-pixel viewport.

The browser checks surfaced two useful bugs. SVGs set to `inline-block` retained line-height space beneath them, while `display: block` produced true square icon controls. Firefox also revealed that Normalize’s line-height made the submit button shorter than its neighboring inputs, so I normalized those controls explicitly. I then designed a mobile navigation that drops down from the top. A single `menu-active` body class translates the drawer by its own height, changes visibility for assistive technology, swaps access between the open and close buttons and will let a very small JavaScript click handler update `aria-expanded`. I finished by testing Animate.css classes and confirming that its page-load effects are CSS keyframes, not JavaScript.

Both menu buttons toggle one `menu-active` class on the body, while the open button’s `aria-expanded` value stays synchronized with the visible state. I tested the menu entirely from the keyboard, confirmed that hidden navigation links are skipped until the user opens the drawer and added Escape-key support so users have another way to close it without trapping focus.

Then I connected the Contact form to Formspree and walked through a real testing process. I added the endpoint, corrected input colors and missing `name` attributes, captured the source URL and path in hidden fields, added an accessible honeypot, checked form validity and disabled the submit button after a successful submission. We verified the payload inside Formspree, waited through a delayed email notification, confirmed that replying targets the visitor’s address and repeated the test on a physical phone. I finished by generating the copyright year in JavaScript and rebuilding the inner-page heading so long titles wrap cleanly above a centered pseudo-element border.

Topics covered:

- Toggling a mobile-navigation body class with vanilla JavaScript
- Keeping `aria-expanded` synchronized with the menu state
- Testing navigation order and behavior with only a keyboard
- Closing an open navigation drawer with the Escape key
- Connecting a static contact form to a Formspree endpoint
- Testing forms in development and production environments
- Fixing input colors, placeholders, buttons and missing names
- Capturing the page URL and path with hidden form fields
- Adding an accessible honeypot to help identify spam
- Checking form validity and preventing duplicate submissions
- Generating a dynamic copyright year in the footer
- Supporting long page titles with a CSS pseudo-element border

This video is for frontend developers who want a practical example of accessible navigation, third-party form handling and careful browser testing without a framework. Subscribe for the next Scenic stream, where I’ll connect the newsletter form to Mailchimp, refine page-load animations, explore a parallax treatment and fix the inner-page logo link.

title: Building a Blog Post Page with Accessible Share Buttons | Part 7
description:
Today I started Scenic’s final page: a responsive blog article template. I replaced the copied homepage content with a semantic article structure containing a featured image, a unique H1, category information, a real `time` element, author metadata, article copy and a dedicated navigation region for sharing. I also constrained unpredictable featured images with `aspect-ratio` and `object-fit`, then refined the title and metadata so the template stays consistent across screen sizes.

Most of the stream focuses on building six accessible sharing controls for Facebook, X, Pinterest, LinkedIn, email and print. I added inline SVGs, hid decorative icons from assistive technology, kept platform names available to screen readers, added official brand colors as CSS variables and arranged the links with Flexbox. The hover, focus and active states required careful control of SVG `fill`, `stroke`, parent classes, specificity and transitions. A tempting `!important` fix turned out to be unnecessary once I found that `stroke="none"` had been added to the wrong X icon.

Topics covered:

- Turning a copied homepage into a semantic blog article template
- Structuring featured images, headings, metadata and article copy
- Using category spans, author labels and the HTML time element

- Constraining featured images with aspect ratio and object fit
- Styling a responsive sharing list with Flexbox
- Transitioning link backgrounds, text, SVG fills and strokes
- Using parent classes to target platform-specific hover states
- Debugging specificity before reaching for `!important`

This video is for frontend developers who want to build resilient blog layouts, accessible icon controls and polished interaction states with semantic HTML and vanilla CSS. title: Connecting a Custom Newsletter Form to Mailchimp | Part 8
description:
Today I connected Scenic’s custom newsletter form to Mailchimp without replacing my markup and styling with Mailchimp’s large embed block. I created the embedded form in Mailchimp, extracted its action endpoint, matched the required `EMAIL` and `FNAME` field names, kept the platform-specific bot trap and reused my existing validation and disabled-submit behavior. After deploying to GitHub Pages, I tested subscriptions on a phone, verified that new contacts reached the audience and discovered that the confirmation flow still needed a corrected custom redirect.

The second half is a practical QA pass. I limited blog copy to roughly 80 characters per line, allowed the social-sharing controls to wrap naturally and used a media query where clamping did not produce the desired mobile padding. I replaced the bouncy test animation with subtle fade-in and fade-in-up effects, standardized border radii, added blur to the homepage hero, corrected inner-page logo paths and fixed an H1 that should have been a non-heading logo element. The unfinished Mailchimp redirect became a useful standalone-video idea rather than something to hide.

title: Accessible Blog Cards with Image Zoom Hover Effects | Part 9
description:
Today I made Scenic’s six homepage article cards behave like production content. I assigned unique images and useful alt text, wrapped each entire card in a block-level anchor, moved the border and radius to the element actually controlled by CSS Grid and added an image-zoom transition for hover, focus and active states. Then I stress-tested different title lengths, tightened the padding, adjusted the fluid font size and line height and refined the mobile section spacing so the cards remain balanced with real editorial content.

The second half is an honest attempt to build a true parallax effect with CSS only. I first demonstrated the common fixed-background version, then researched the 3D technique using `perspective`, `transform-style`, `translateZ()`, scaling, overflow and pseudo-elements. We rebuilt the markup into background and static layers and got close to the intended composition, but the layers still did not scroll at visibly different speeds. Rather than copy a creator’s tutorial live without permission or pretend the effect was finished, I left the experiment in progress and committed to studying it offline before the next stream.

Topics covered:

- Replacing repeated card images with six unique scenic assets
- Writing concise, meaningful alt text for editorial images
- Wrapping an entire content card in a block-level anchor
- Moving Grid item styles to the new anchor container
- Zooming card images on hover, focus and active states
- Containing transformed images with `overflow: hidden`
- Stress-testing headings with realistic title lengths
- Refining mobile font size, line height, padding and alignment
- Comparing fixed-background and true parallax effects
- Weighing background-image tradeoffs for accessibility and SEO
- Researching perspective, `translateZ()`, scale and 3D layers
- Knowing when to pause debugging and study a technique offline

This video is for frontend developers who want to see how small semantic and interaction details make content cards more resilient—and how to handle an unfamiliar CSS technique honestly when it does not work on the first attempt. Subscribe for the next Scenic stream, where I’ll return with the corrected parallax approach and build dynamic social-sharing links.

description:

I styled a responsive content panel over the image, reused and generalized button styles, checked the text contrast against a translucent blue background, and added a dotted pseudo-element border plus `backdrop-filter` blur. title: Dynamic Social Share Links with Vanilla JavaScript | Part 11
description:
Today I finished Scenic’s blog tools with vanilla JavaScript. I changed the print control from an anchor to a real button, connected it to `window.print()` and debugged a naming collision between the selected element and its initialization function. Then I added a compact `@media print` stylesheet that switches to a basic font stack, normalizes paragraph and link colors and hides the header, footer and sharing navigation while leaving printer margins and color options under the user’s control.

The main build turns five hard coded share URLs into a reusable page-driven component. The script reads the current URL, pulls the H1 text, finds the featured image, converts its source to an absolute path, encodes the values and assigns complete Facebook, X, Pinterest, LinkedIn and `mailto:` destinations. Pinterest receives the image and title, while email receives a prefilled subject and body. After a useful refactor suggested in chat, I encoded the complete endpoint strings at assignment time, deployed the changes and confirmed every share target and the print view on the hosted site.

Topics covered:

- Fixing a pseudo-element that blocked clicks with pointer events

title: Deploy a Static Site with Apache, DNS and SSL on DigitalOcean | Part 12
description:
Today I deployed the completed Scenic website to `scenic.practicelayouts.com` on an existing DigitalOcean LAMP droplet. I created matching A records with my registrar and DigitalOcean, connected over SSH, updated the server, created the new `public_html` directory and set its ownership and permissions. Then I uploaded only the production files through FileZilla, created and enabled the Apache port 80 virtual host, reloaded Apache and used Certbot to generate and install the Let’s Encrypt SSL configuration.

The first deployment exposed two missing steps in my new documentation: copying the base virtual-host file and enabling the site before running Certbot. I corrected the mental model, verified HTTP-to-HTTPS redirects and status codes and diagnosed a misleading Chrome result as cached state by retesting in Incognito, Firefox and Safari. To reinforce the process, I deployed the archived Solo Masonry project as a second subdomain and updated the Practice Layouts directory. Finally, I ran production QA on navigation, Formspree submissions from desktop and mobile, reply-to email behavior, every social share destination and the print view.

Topics covered:

- Pointing a subdomain to a DigitalOcean droplet with A records
- Separating domain registration from cloud hosting
- Connecting to a LAMP server with SSH and a sudo user
- Creating `public_html` directories and setting permissions
- Uploading only required production files with FileZilla
- Creating and editing an Apache port 80 virtual host
- Enabling a site and reloading Apache before Certbot
- Installing a Let’s Encrypt certificate for HTTPS
- Testing 301 redirects and 200 responses with command-line tools
- Distinguishing a real deployment bug from browser caching
- Repeating the workflow for a second archived project
- Testing forms, email replies, sharing, printing and mobile

This video is for frontend developers who want to understand what one-click deployment tools abstract away and learn to host multiple static sites securely on one affordable server. Subscribe for the next live stream, where I’ll choose a new multi-page design from the archive and begin another vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript build.

title: How I Start a Web Design Before Writing Any Code | Part 1
description:
Today I paused the Colorado build and started designing the website for my upcoming 30 Days of Vanilla JavaScript challenge. Beginning April 1, I’ll solve one JavaScript prompt every day, build a usable interface around it and deploy the result to a permanent learning resource. To make that daily workflow sustainable, the site needs a repeatable page template, a 30-day navigation system, room for the prompt and completed UI, Prism-highlighted code and a structure that can be deployed immediately after each stream.

Instead of opening a blank artboard and inventing a homepage all at once, I built a style guide in Affinity Photo. I chose and installed Oswald, found an MIT-licensed JavaScript logo on Wikimedia Commons, generated palettes from the logo yellow, tested every important combination for WCAG contrast, rejected the first purple-and-green direction and rebuilt the palette around three teal shades and a soft gray. From there I defined typography, hollow and solid buttons, a Prism code block, a three-column 30-day navigation, current-page treatment, header icons, component area and footer. We finished by confirming with ChatGPT that the root URL can serve as both the homepage and day one while later days use their own paths.

title: Building a Sticky Sidebar Layout with Flexbox | Part 3
description:
Today I focused on the CSS layout for the 30 Days of Vanilla JavaScript website, but I started by auditing the kitchen-sink markup ChatGPT generated yesterday. Its `aria-labelledby` attributes were valid but redundant because each section already had a real heading. I removed that defensive, noisy ARIA and explained why native semantic HTML should do the work until a component genuinely needs additional accessibility information.

From there I built the responsive header, social navigation and main two-column layout. I created 48-by-48-pixel tap targets around smaller SVG icons, added focus and hover states, made the header sticky and compared `position: sticky` with `position: fixed`. The day navigation became a 400-pixel sticky column beside a flexible section container, which required restructuring the markup, checking whether the site footer belonged inside `main` and accepting some unfinished layout questions instead of polishing too early. I finished by styling the page title with `clamp()`, testing whether a body font size changes `rem` measurements and confirming that `rem` follows the root `html` font size instead.

Topics covered:

- Auditing AI-generated markup instead of trusting it blindly
- Removing redundant `aria-labelledby` attributes from semantic sections

title: Testing Three CSS Accordion Animation Techniques | Part 4
description:
Today I styled the shared UI that will support the first ten prompts in my 30 Days of Vanilla JavaScript project. I reduced the button system to a solid and an outline style, tested their contrast, replaced the overly bright navy palette with muted accessible blues, and finalized three rotating page themes: teal, navy, and pink. Then I wired those themes through the header, social-icon states, sidebar, buttons, alternating sections, and footer while using DevTools to explain why selector specificity can override rules that appear later in a stylesheet.

I also turned the starter page into a “day zero” component playground and added responsive section spacing, heading rules, labels, text areas, and shared input styles. The second half became a detailed accordion experiment: I made each heading button fill its entire clickable region, kept collapsed content away from screen readers, and tested `max-height`, CSS Grid rows, `calc-size()`, and `interpolate-size`. The newer intrinsic-size features were not supported broadly enough, the Grid approach did not fit this markup, and padding made the close animation jump. The practical result was a simpler `max-height` and visibility transition, with spacing moved outside the animated panel so the behavior could determine the final visual design.

Topics covered:

- Preparing shared CSS so daily streams can focus on JavaScript
- Simplifying the design to solid and outline button variants
- Checking button text, borders, and backgrounds for contrast
- Replacing bright blues with a muted accessible navy palette
- Rotating teal, navy, and pink themes across 30 pages
- Debugging theme overrides with CSS specificity in DevTools
- Creating alternating component sections with `:nth-child()`
- Styling labels, text areas, and common form input types
- Keeping global element styles minimal and using component classes
- Making accordion trigger buttons full-width and left-aligned
- Comparing `max-height`, Grid, `calc-size()`, and `interpolate-size`
- Coordinating visibility, overflow, spacing, and accordion animation

This video is for frontend developers who want a realistic look at reusable CSS component work, including accessibility checks, browser support research, discarded approaches, and the small layout details that affect interactive behavior. title: Building an Accessible Modal with the HTML Dialog Element | Part 5
description:
Today I continued preparing the reusable interface for 30 Days of Vanilla JavaScript, starting with an accessibility test of the accordion from the previous stream. By adding a real link to a collapsed panel and tabbing through the page, I confirmed that `visibility: hidden` keeps hidden content out of both keyboard focus and the screen reader’s path. I then added plus and minus SVG controls with screen-reader-only labels, worked through the sizing and line-height math behind consistent 48-pixel targets, and gave each accordion trigger a plus icon that rotates when its parent receives an active class.

Topics covered:

- Why small vanilla projects improve CSS specificity and inheritance skills
- Testing hidden accordion content with keyboard focus
- Using `visibility: hidden` for assistive-technology behavior
- Adding screen-reader labels to icon-only SVG buttons
- Removing inline SVG stroke values for CSS control
- Aligning text and icon buttons with line height and fixed tap targets
- Rotating an accordion indicator from its active parent state

- Comparing `show()`, `showModal()`, and the `open` attribute

title: Grouping and Expanding API Search Results with JavaScript | Part 6
description:

title: Using AI to Refine an E-Reader Backend | Part 4
description:
Today I built and tested the importer for my Jane Austen database, but the first real import uncovered an architectural problem worth solving before publishing the SQLite database. The importer found all six books and 269 chapters, and all 11 automated tests passed, but sentence counts differed across 62 chapters. Instead of forcing the tokenizer to reproduce undocumented sentence boundaries, I stepped back and reconsidered what the application actually needs.

I decided that paragraphs are a better canonical search chunk for this e-reader. They preserve useful context, support exact-phrase search and frontend highlighting, and avoid ambiguous rules around dialogue, abbreviations, ellipses and historical punctuation. I also traced the remaining paragraph mismatches to Gutenberg illustration blocks and defined a concrete parsing rule: exclude decorative content, but preserve it as a structural separator so surrounding prose never merges.
